title: Brain Teasers Arcade
intro: Six rounds on microcontrollers, pins, digital signals and PWM. Get them right first try to earn ⭐⭐⭐!

rounds.prompt: What's the single biggest difference between a microcontroller and your laptop?
options: A microcontroller runs one program forever and has no screen; a laptop runs many programs with rich input/output
rounds.explain: A microcontroller is built for one narrow job, cheaply and on almost no power — very different goals from a general-purpose computer.

rounds.prompt: Match each pin type to its job.

pairs.right: You choose in code: read input or write output
Supplies a steady 3.3V, for small loads only
Pulling it low resets the board

rounds.explain: Four kinds of pin, four different jobs. GPIO is the flexible one — everything else is fixed.

rounds.prompt: Why does the ESP32 matter more for this course than a basic Arduino Uno?
options: It has built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, which later modules rely on for remote control and voice features
It's the only board that can run any code at all
rounds.explain: ARIA's brain needs wireless later in the course. The ESP32 has it built in with no extra parts.

rounds.prompt: A digital GPIO pin reads either HIGH or LOW. What voltage roughly counts as LOW?
rounds.explain: LOW means close to 0V. HIGH means close to the board's operating voltage. There's no in-between reading.

rounds.prompt: An LED is driven with PWM at 80% duty cycle. What does that actually mean is happening?
options: The pin genuinely outputs 80% of full voltage
The pin is fully HIGH for 80% of each cycle and fully LOW for the rest — never in between
The LED itself is dimming its own brightness
rounds.explain: PWM never leaves HIGH/LOW. It fakes an in-between brightness purely by controlling the fraction of time spent HIGH.

rounds.prompt: Why does PWM need a fast enough frequency to work as a dimmer?
options: So the on/off flips are too fast to perceive, and only the average brightness registers
Frequency has nothing to do with it, only duty cycle matters
rounds.explain: Slow the frequency down (as the widget lets you) and you stop seeing a dimmer light — you see it blinking, one flip at a time.
